UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.             )                      Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                )                      Docket No. EL25-49-001
                                                )
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities )                      Docket No. AD24-11-000
                                                )
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC            )                      Docket No. EL25-20-000
      v.                                        )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                     )                      (Consolidated)


                                  JOINT RESPONSE OF
                       THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS


        Pursuant to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 order in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.,

193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order”), the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (collectively the

“PJM Transmission Owners”)1 submit this joint response to the initial brief filed by PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) on February 23, 2026 (“PJM Initial Brief”).




1
          For the purpose of this filing, the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky
Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian
Transmission Company, AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, AEP Kentucky Transmission Company,
AEP Ohio Transmission Company, and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company; The Dayton Power and Light
Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a
Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy
Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its
affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company,
Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company , and
Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission
Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The
Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and
Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities
Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland
Electric Cooperative.
 I.      INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND

        In the Order, the Commission ordered PJM to offer three new forms of transmission service

under its Tariff: (i) Firm Contract Demand transmission service; (ii) Non-Firm Contract Demand

transmission service and (iii) interim, non-firm transmission service under the PJM Open Access

Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) for Eligible Customers2 serving co-located load in PJM.3 The

Commission also established this paper hearing process to determine the just and reasonable rates,

terms, and conditions for these new transmission services.4 For the paper hearing process, the

Commission provided for initial briefs, responses to initial briefs and replies to those responses.5

The PJM Transmission Owners are submitting this response in order to reply to PJM’s Initial Brief

filed on February 23, 2026.

        In the PJM Initial Brief, PJM addresses the paper hearing questions posed in the Order

regarding non-rate terms and conditions associated with the three new transmission services

required by the Commission.6 The PJM Initial Brief also contains supporting affidavits, along

with illustrative tariff records (“Illustrative Tariff”), containing tariff provisions to implement

PJM’s proposed terms and conditions. The PJM Transmission Owners applaud PJM on the

substantial progress it has made in a short time towards developing the non-rate terms and

conditions required to effectuate the new transmission services and support the general structure

for effectuating those services that PJM proposes in the PJM Initial Brief. Moreover, assuming

 that the new transmission services are ultimately required to be implemented, an action with which

some PJM Transmission Owners strongly disagree, the PJM Transmission Owners agree that most

of the modifications and new provisions that PJM proposes to include in its Tariff are just and

reasonable. This response focuses on a limited number of items that require clarification or modest

changes, or where additional detail is necessary.

II.     JOINT RESPONSE TO PJM’s INITIAL BRIEF

        A.       Issues Relating to the Interaction Between Firm Contract Demand Service
                 and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service.

        In the PJM Initial Brief, PJM states that for an Eligible Customer taking Contract Demand

Service, the portion of the Co-Located Load for which a co-located generating facility will dedicate

its output may be covered by Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service and any portion

of the gross demand of a Co-Located Load that is not covered by a co-located generating facility

must be covered by Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service.7 In total, the cumulative amount

of Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service must equal the entire gross demand

of the Co-Located Load.8 This approach is reflected in PJM’s Illustrative Tariff, which would

require an Eligible Customer applying for Contract Demand Service to apply for a combination of

Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to cover the Co-Located Load’s entire

gross load.9




7
         PJM Initial Brief at 6-7. In their initial brief, the PJM Transmission Owners refer to Firm and Non-Firm
Contract Demand Services (“PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief”). For purposes of this response, the PJM
Transmission Owners have adopted the terms for these services used in the PJM Initial Brief: Firm and Non-Firm
Contract Demand Transmission Services.
8
        PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 709.2.
9
        PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 710.2.

                                                        3
        The PJM Transmission Owners support these basic requirements but further clarification

is necessary. First, based on the materials provided in the PJM Initial Brief,10 as well as subsequent

stakeholder presentations made by PJM, it appears that PJM contemplates that an Eligible

Customer’s initial application for a certain amount of Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service would essentially serve as a “holding” request, and the actual reservation and use of Non-

Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service would require the Eligible Customer to submit

individual requests for service in advance of the interval during which it wishes to obtain such

service. For instance, if an Eligible Customer’s co-located generator will be on scheduled outage

for a month, the Eligible Customer would be required to request, in advance of that month, Non-

Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service for that month, at which point PJM would determine

whether or not the requested amount of Non-Firm service is available. Moreover, the amount that

PJM determines is available for a particular requested interval or intervals would presumably serve

as the basis for determining the relevant charge to the Eligible Customer for Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service. PJM should confirm these understandings are correct and add

appropriate language to its proposed Tariff provisions.

       Moreover, PJM should clarify pertinent details relating to this process. For instance,

Section 710.3 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff sets forth a study process to determine what levels of

Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service can be provided to an Eligible

Customer. However, it is not clear if this process is meant to cover only the initial service study,

or also subsequent determinations as to available Non-Firm capacity based on specific reservation

requests. Regardless, more detail should be provided as to the process for evaluating and granting

specific reservation requests for Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, including the


10
       PJM Initial Brief at 9-10, Attachment B at 5-6.

                                                         4
 timelines associated with such requests. For instance, PJM explains that Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service is available only when a generating facility dedicated to serving

Co-Located Load is on outage, but it is not clear what reservation requirements and timelines

would apply to forced outages. Based on the Order,11 the PJM Transmission Owners assume that

Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service will be available for periods from one month

to one hour in duration, but this should be specified in the relevant PJM Tariff language.

       B.       The Study Process for Co-Located Load Arrangements Should be Clarified to
                Recognize the Priority of Load Integration Studies.

       In its Initial Brief, PJM proposes a study process for Contract Demand Transmission

Service whereby PJM will determine, in accordance with PJM Manuals, any studies necessary to

provide the requested transmission service.12 For Interim Network Integration Transmission

Service (“NITS”), PJM will determine whether additional studies beyond those required to

evaluate the Eligible Customer’s request for NITS are needed for Interim NITS.13 If additional

studies are required, PJM will inform the Eligible Customer and then tender to the customer an

application and study agreement within 15 days. PJM’s proposal appropriately recognizes the

important role of the affected PJM Transmission Owner(s) in evaluating load interconnection

requests, stating that PJM will notify the affected PJM Transmission Owner(s) after receiving an

application for Contract Demand Transmission Service or Interim NITS, and specifying that if

studies are required, it will consider the results of any studies conducted by the PJM Transmission

Owners.14 This approach serves as a just and reasonable foundation for studying Contract Demand




11
       See Order at P 215.
12
       PJM Initial Brief at 24-25.
13
       PJM Initial Brief at 70-71.
14
       PJM Initial Brief at 24, 68.

                                                 5
 Transmission Service or Interim NITS requests, but more detail should be added to clarify that the

load integration studies conducted by the PJM Transmission Owners will be conducted first and

inform any studies required by PJM relating to an Eligible Customer’s request for transmission

service and co-located generation interconnection.

       As the PJM Transmission Owners explained in their initial brief, they will still need to

perform load integration studies for any Co-Located Load arrangements, similar to what they do

today with respect to any large load customers, but with an expanded study scope due to the

addition of co-located generation.15 Nothing in PJM’s proposal prevents the PJM Transmission

Owners from conducting these necessary large load analyses to ensure local reliability. To the

contrary, PJM’s Illustrative Tariff provisions specifically indicate that PJM “will coordinate with

the affected Transmission Owner(s) to complete studies, including load integration studies, which

will provide data relevant to the determination of whether (and to what level as applicable)”

requested Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service can be provided.16

       The PJM Transmission Owners support this approach. It is critically important that PJM

and the PJM Transmission Owners work closely and collaboratively in order to ensure that large

loads, including those co-located with generation, can be quickly and efficiently interconnected.

The PJM Transmission Owners are fully committed to achieving this goal. However, more detail

is necessary as to how a PJM Transmission Owner’s load integration studies will be sequenced

with Eligible Customer requests to PJM for Contract Demand and Interim NITS Transmission

Services, as well as any related generator interconnection studies. The Tariff should specify that

Transmission Owners’ load integration studies will be completed first and thereby inform the



15
       PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief at 25-26.
16
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 710.3 (emphasis added).

                                                      6
 determination of whether and what additional studies are necessary for purposes of an Eligible

Customer’s request for transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located Load and the

interconnection of any on-site generation. Transmission Owners will always need to study new

load additions to ensure that they can be reliably interconnected to the grid, regardless of the type

of transmission service being requested. Any facilities that the Transmission Owners determines

are necessary to reliably interconnect the load can inform additional transmission and generation

studies. Therefore, conducting load integration studies first will maximize the speed and efficiency

of the overall process and avoid potential duplication of effort and expense between the PJM

Transmission Owners and PJM.

       C.      PJM’s Proposed Provisions Relating to Necessary Control Technologies and
               Protection Systems Should Be Clarified and Expanded.

       PJM’s proposal appropriately includes requirements for necessary control technologies and

protective systems in order to protect the transmission system and limit an Eligible Customer’s

withdrawals. Pursuant to these requirements, the Transmission Provider, affected Transmission

Owner(s) and Eligible Customer shall establish the necessary control technologies and protection

systems for each service agreement.17 The PJM Transmission Owners request two clarifications

to these provisions.

       First, PJM should make clear that in order for an Eligible Customer to take any form of

new transmission services, whether it be Interim NITS, or Firm or Non-Firm Contract Demand,

the customer must comply with requirements to implement necessary control technologies and

protection systems. Currently, PJM’s proposed Tariff language refers to such requirements in the

context of Interim NITS and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, but not Firm




17
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Sections 705.5 and 713.6.

                                                      7
 Contract Demand Transmission Service.18 It is important, however, that each new transmission

service be conditioned, as determined through studies of each individual customer’s arrangements,

on the implementation of control technologies and protection systems to ensure that a Co-Located

Load does not exceed its specified level of transmission service. This is because PJM will only be

planning and operating the system to reliably accommodate the contractually specified level of

transmission service.

        The PJM Transmission Owners appreciate that PJM’s proposal will require an Eligible

Customer to take a combination of Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to

cover its entire gross load when co-located generation is unavailable. However, regardless of the

type of services being taken, necessary control technology and system protections must be

implemented. Therefore, in order to avoid confusion regarding an Eligible Customer’s obligations,

PJM should add language to its Illustrative Tariff provisions making clear that Interim NITS, as

well as both Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, are contingent on the

implementation of necessary control technologies and protection systems, where applicable.

        Second, PJM should modify the Illustrative Tariff provisions to make clear that necessary

control technologies and protection systems may (some would say should) be required on the

customer’s side or both the customer’s side and the Transmission Owner’s side of the point of

interconnection. As the PJM Transmission Owners explained in their initial brief, the use of

control technologies and protection systems to protect the grid from large amounts of on-site load

exceeding their contractual withdrawal limitations, whether on an instantaneous, shorter-term, or



18
         See, e.g., PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 708 (“Prior to the Commencement of Service, for an
Eligible Customer to take Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service on behalf of a Co-Located Load, the
Eligible Customer must demonstrate the implementation of the necessary control technologies and protection systems,
approved by the Transmission Provider to allow the Eligible Customer to effectively limit withdrawals from the
Transmission System to serve such Co-Located Load.”) (emphasis added).

                                                        8
 longer-term basis, rather than building more permanent transmission solutions, is novel.19 This

approach will require providing Transmission Owners with flexibility to determine how best to

ensure reliability on their respective systems, including whether contractual limitations agreed to

by Co-Located Load customers are best secured by control technologies and protection systems

on only the Co-Located Load side or on both the Co-Located Load and independently on the

Transmission Owner side of the point of interconnection. PJM’s Tariff provisions should be

sufficiently broad to encompass both approaches.20

         In addition to these clarifications, additional detail will need to be developed to further

define the requirements associated with the control technologies and protection systems necessary

to ensure that Co-Located Loads do not exceed their relevant withdrawal limitations. The PJM

Transmission Owners recognize that PJM is planning to include further details on this issue in

PJM Manuals, but regardless of where this detail resides, it is important that PJM work closely

with the PJM Transmission Owners and other stakeholders to develop this detail so that all parties

understand their respective rights and obligations. In their initial brief, the PJM Transmission

Owners suggested a number of criteria relating to the use of control technologies and protection

systems, and the PJM Transmission Owners urge PJM and the Commission to adopt these criteria,

to the extent they are not already contained in PJM’s proposal.21

         The PJM Transmission Owners understand that PJM is considering, in other stakeholder

initiatives, questions regarding potential study priorities for large loads that bring their own



19
         PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief at 23-24.
20
         See, e.g., PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 702.5 (noting that the provision of “Interim NITS”
service will be conditioned upon the “Eligible Customer constructing, maintaining, and operating the facilities on its
side of the Delivery Point necessary to reliably deliver capacity and energy from the Transmission Provider’s
Transmission System to the Eligible Customer”).
21
         PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief at 23-24.

                                                          9
 generation. Any such priority process should ensure that its interaction with the new transmission

services does not create opportunities for customers to game the system; for instance, by adding

de minimis amounts of co-located generation to trigger the priority, or by taking Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service equal to their entire on-site load to gain a priority over NITS

customers.

        Finally, it is important to recognize that, based on recent discussions at the NERC Large

Load Technical Conference, regulatory expectations for emerging large loads are evolving. At

that conference, NERC and other reliability organizations indicated they are considering extending

certain reliability standards currently applicable to generation owners to large load customers,

reflecting their view that these facilities increasingly function as grid infrastructure rather than

traditional end use customers.22 This process is of key importance because currently there is no

compliance entity on the load side to tie to NERC obligations, resulting in significant potential

liability and exposure to Transmission Owners and other entities with defined NERC obligations,

as well as increased risks to system reliability

        D.       Development of Telemetry Requirements.

        In its Initial Brief, PJM states that to ensure adequate reliability and stability of PJM’s

Transmission System, it expects to develop telemetry requirements and require Co-Located Load

to meet such requirements in order to monitor Co-Located Load’s use of the transmission system.23

The PJM Transmission Owners support PJM’s proposal to develop and implement telemetry

requirements as described in the Initial Brief.24 Such requirements are an important reliability

       See, e.g., NERC, Assessment of Gaps in Existing Practices, Requirements, and Reliability Standards for
Emerging Large Loads (Feb. 24, 2026), https://www.nysrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/NYSRC-LLWG-3-Att.-
1-NERC-LLWG-Tech-Conference-Presentations.pdf at 63-70.
23
        PJM Initial Brief at 59.
24
        PJM Initial Brief at 59-61.

                                                     10
 measure and are consistent with broader developments at the North American Electric Reliability

Council (“NERC”), as discussed above.

       E.       Penalties for Unreserved Use.

       In its Initial Brief, PJM proposes operational penalties for Eligible Customers taking

Interim NITS or Contract Demand Service that would apply when: (i) an Eligible Customer fails

to follow established Load Shedding and Curtailment procedures; or (ii) necessary control

technology and protection systems misoperate.25           For the first instance of a control

technology/protection system misoperation, PJM proposes a 120 day pause in service, which may

be shortened or extended by mutual agreement. The PJM Transmission Owners strongly urge that

the relevant Transmission Owner’s approval must be included in the process of allowing service

to be reinstated, and this requirement should be added to the Tariff language. Upon a second

misoperation, or if an Eligible Customer fails to follow Load Shedding and Curtailment procedures

even once, PJM proposes a strict liability rule resulting in the disqualification of an Interim NITS

customer thereby forcing them to take traditional NITS or forcing a customer taking a Contract

Demand Service to then take either Interim NITS or traditional NITS.26

       As stated in their initial brief, the PJM Transmission Owners agree with PJM that the

imposition of operational penalties is appropriate, but also believe that any penalty regime should

rely on both operational consequences and complementary financial penalties.27 In its Initial Brief,

PJM states that it supports a financial penalty for unreserved use, and intends to work with the

PJM Transmission Owners to explore such a financial penalty.28 The PJM Transmission Owners



25
       PJM Initial Brief at 40.
26
       PJM Initial Brief at 41-46.
27
       PJM Transmission Owners Initial Brief at 19-20.
28
       PJM Initial Brief at 50-51.

                                                     11
 appreciate and agree with PJM’s comments on this issue, and propose a financial penalty charge

structure with two components: (1) a base penalty charge, which applies to each individual hour

in which the reserved transmission service limit is exceeded, and (2) a penalty ratchet, which

applies when such exceedances occur repeatedly. The PJM Transmission Owners provide a basic

outline of this proposal below, with more details forthcoming in future filings in this proceeding.

In addition to this proposed penalty for unreserved use, the PJM Transmission Owners propose to

apply financial penalties in instances in which a Co-Located Load fails to curtail upon instruction.

The PJM Transmission Owners will also provide additional details on this proposal in future

filings.

           When a Co-Located Load exceeds its reserved transmission service limit, the base penalty

charge will be assessed for any hour in which at least one five-minute interval occurs during which

a customer’s metered load at the point of interconnection exceeds its reserved transmission service.

Such a five-minute interval is defined as an Exceedance Interval, and such an hour is defined as

an Exceedance Hour. The base penalty charge will apply to each Exceedance Hour. The penalty

rachet applies when multiple Exceedance Hours occur during a particular time period. It is

designed to discourage recurring reliance on unreserved transmission capacity.

           Under the penalty rachet framework, the penalty charges escalate as the frequency of

unreserved transmission use increases. Specifically, if more than one Exceedance Hour occurs on

the same day, an additional daily penalty applies. If exceedances occur on multiple days within

the same week, an additional weekly penalty applies; likewise, if exceedances occur in multiple

weeks within the same month, an additional monthly penalty applies. Each of these penalties will

involve escalating financial liabilities for prolonged periods of time. By progressively increasing

the economic consequences of repeated penalties, the penalty ratchet reinforces the expectation



                                                  12
 that Co-Located Load customers manage their load in a manner consistent with their reserved

transmission service.

        F.      Comments on Specific Proposed Tariff Provisions.

        In addition to the general comments set forth above, the PJM Transmission Owners have

identified a number of suggested modifications or requests for clarification relating to the

Illustrative Tariff records proposed by PJM.

                1.       Interim Network Integrated Transmission Service Provisions.

                         a.       Section 702.4 – Technical Requirements Prior to
                                  Commencement of Service.

        Section 702.4 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff states that the Eligible Customer must (i) install

“necessary hardware and software to limit energy withdrawals, including metering equipment;”

(ii) provide PJM an operational contact and backup contact that is to be available 24 hours a day

and 7 days a week, (iii) certify that it “is staffed with PJM Certified Operators pursuant to PJM

Manual 40;” (iv) demonstrate “its ability to receive voice and electronic signals from [PJM];” (v)

demonstrate that it “has operational control to respond to operating instructions from [PJM] to

reduce or disconnect the Co-Located Load within 5 minutes or as specified in PJM Manuals;” and

(vi) demonstrate that it “has operational control of the necessary control technologies and

protection systems set forth in . . . section 705, as applicable.”29

        These technical requirements should also require an Eligible Customer to satisfy any

applicable Transmission Owner-imposed technical requirements. As the entities managing the

load interconnection process, including any load integration studies, the PJM Transmission

Owners will play a key role in ensuring the technical sufficiency of Co-Located Load connections

and operations.


29
        PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 702.4.

                                                       13
                         b.       Section 703.2 – New Co-Located Loads Connected with the
                                 Transmission Provider.

       Section 703.2 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff states:

       Prior to the Service Commencement Date of Network Integration Transmission Service, if
       an Eligible Customer designates a new Co-Located Load, or increases the size of the
       designated Co-Located Load, the new Co-Located Load shall be studied pursuant to a new
       Application.30

       In order to fully account for increases in the size of the designated Co-Located Load, the

PJM Transmission Owners propose the following revision to Section 703.2.

       Prior to the Service Commencement Date of Network Integration Transmission Service, if
       an Eligible Customer designates a new Co-Located Load, or increases the size of the
       designated Co-Located Load, the new or increased Co-Located Load shall be studied
       pursuant to a new Application.

                        c.       Section 703.3 – Information Updates.

       Under Section 703.3 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff, in order to maintain operational visibility

by PJM of the system and thus to ensure reliability, Eligible Customers will have an ongoing

obligation to provide the Transmission Provider with timely written or electronic notice of material

changes in the demand characteristics of the Co-Located Load and the supply characteristics of

the Co-Located Generating Facility.31 PJM, however, does not indicate how or where the term

“material change” will be defined.

       PJM should provide additional information as to what would constitute a “material change”

in the demand characteristics of the Co-Located Load, particularly with respect to: (i) large, but

foreseeable, load ramps that occur on a defined or scheduled basis; and (ii) the timing requirements

for submitting a new application once such changes are anticipated or occur.




30
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 703.2.
31
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 703.3.

                                                      14
                         d.       Section 705.3 – Load Shedding.

       PJM proposes that to the extent a contingency requires Transmission Owners and Eligible

Customers taking Interim NITS to shed load, such load shedding shall occur in accordance with

previously established procedures as set forth in the relevant transmission service agreement and

PJM Manuals.32 There should be load shedding practice guidelines applicable to Co-Located Load

arrangements established by PJM. Such load shedding guidelines will make it less complicated

and more efficient for PJM to manage Co-Located Load arrangements. Such practices will also

ensure that Co-Located Load customers will understand the relevant process when they seek to

connect and their load shedding priority when they are withdrawing energy from the grid.

       The PJM Transmission Owners are particularly concerned with automatic load shedding

schemes. If a large load were to suddenly appear due to a forced outage of a Co-Located Load’s

on-site generation, even a fast disconnection by the customer could cause issues if the

disconnection is not fast enough. With large loads rapidly looking to interconnect coupled with

the retirement of synchronous generation facilities, the lack of inertia may cause sudden localized

frequency decline. If such an event occurs near a location where there is an automatic load

shedding scheme, unintentional activation of the automatic load shedding scheme could result in

unwanted shedding of nearby customer loads in addition to the Co-Located Load.

                        e.       Section 705.5 – Necessary Control Technologies and Protection
                                 Systems.

       Section 705.5 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff concerns necessary control technologies and

protection systems and provides:

       To ensure protection of the Transmission System, and to ensure that the Eligible
       Customer taking Interim Network Integration Transmission Service on behalf of a
       Co-Located Load limits its energy withdrawals from the Transmission System to

32
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 705.3.

                                                      15
        its approved level of Interim Network Integration Transmission Service, including
       during a period in which the Transmission Provider has directed Curtailment or
       Load Shedding, prior to the Service Commencement Date, the Transmission
       Provider, affected Transmission Owner(s), and the Eligible Customer shall
       establish necessary control technologies and protection systems in accordance with
       the PJM Manuals, which may include a Remedial Action Scheme, for each Service
       Agreement for Interim Network Integration Transmission Service. The necessary
       control technologies and protection systems must be developed in accordance with
       the PJM Manuals and be approved by the Transmission Provider. The necessary
       control technologies and protection systems may be functionally modified from
       time to time in accordance with the PJM Manuals. Any functional modification to
       the necessary control technologies and protection systems must be developed with
       the affected Transmission Owner(s) and, before taking effect, such functional
       modification must be approved by the Transmission Provider.33

       The PJM Transmission Owners strongly agree with PJM’s proposal to impose necessary

control technologies and protection systems obligations on Eligible Customers.          However,

additional detail is needed on how those obligations will be determined and imposed. For example,

it is not clear whether the obligation to “establish necessary control technologies and protection

systems in accordance with the PJM Manuals,” binds a Transmission Owner to install equipment

itself, or just to enforce the criteria on a Eligible Customer.34 Moreover, the PJM Transmission

Owners believe that the “necessary control technologies and protection systems” that must be

developed in accordance with the PJM Manuals and approved by PJM should also be approved by

and developed in accordance with the PJM Transmission Owners’ interconnection standards,

guidelines, and practices. In addition, to properly address modifications to the necessary control

technologies and protection systems, the PJM Transmission Owners propose the following

revision to Section 705.5:

       Any functional modification to the necessary control technologies and protection
       systems must be developed with the affected Transmission Owner(s) and, before
       taking effect, such functional modification must be approved by the Transmission
       Provider and coordinated with the affected Transmission Owner(s).

33
       PJM Initial Brief at Attachment A, Section 705.5.
34
       Id.

                                                      16
                           f.       Section 706.2 – Redispatch Charge.

        Section 706.2 of PJM’s Illustrative Tariff states that “[t]he Eligible Customer and each

Transmission Owner shall pay any redispatch costs as set forth in Tariff, Attachment K.”35

However, Transmission Owners should not be responsible for redispatch costs because such costs

will be caused by Contract Demand Transmission Service customers. PJM indicated that the

reference to Transmission Owners in Section 706.2 is incorrect. Accordingly, PJM should remove

this reference from any filed tariff records.

        In addition, this provision could result in cost shifts onto other customers because Eligible

Customers may represent multiple load customers.36 Therefore, PJM should either: (1) modify

the curtailment order so that Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service load is curtailed

prior to generation redispatch, or (2) reevaluate the applicability of its redispatch cost allocation
